$comment: labels.byline is "{name} wrote this": the author's name, here the link to their archive, comes first, so a renderer that strips the placeholder and appends the name draws "wrote this Priya Shah" and fails (README "Labels"). The rest is full. document: a post's fields as contract/collections/posts.json defines them, as the post view receives them. Stored as defined: title, featuredImage (media id). Resolved for the view: href; date (YYYY-MM-DD) from publishedAt in site.timezone; category from primaryTopic and topics from topics, each { title, href }, the primary topic first and the rest A to Z (Soil, then Composting); author, the credited team member (contract/collections/team.json) as { name, href?, role, bio, photo (media id) }; body, the layout's one rich-text section that is prose alone (rich-text string, stored h3 renders h2 at base 1; section#sections-in-a-post, and post/band-* for a layout with bands); readingMinutes, share and adjacent, derived. Shapes of site are this case's own (the gate checks only declared site keys): site.home { href, title }, site.collectionIndexes.post { href, title } (the blog index), site.timezone. Share intents are the services' public share URLs for the post's canonical URL. The markup does not say whether the three meta spans are separated; one space is drawn between them. The contract has no site key for showing the breadcrumb, byline, share or author box; each is drawn here because the document supplies its data.

document.title: Feeding your soil, not your plants

author.name: Priya Shah
author.bio: Priya has run the kitchen garden at Hollin Farm for eleven years and writes about soil, water and patience.

document.body:
Most gardeners reach for a bottle of feed the moment leaves turn pale. The soil is usually the better place to start.

Why compost does the heavy lifting

A well-rotted mulch feeds the organisms that feed your plants, and it holds water through a dry spell.

Spread it two inches deep each autumn and leave the worms to do the digging. See our guide to hedge laying for the other end of the garden.
